2026-10-18.q: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
opts: The Rotunda Hospital has lost its funding.
The HSE says consultants have stopped private work in public hospitals, though questions remain about enforcement and cost.
Consultants have been banned from all private work in Ireland.
Private maternity hospitals are being built to replace public ones.
2026-10-18.exp: The passage reports the HSE's finding, then raises Rice's doubts about enforcement and the €145 million shortfall. The ban applies only in public settings (C); the Rotunda board conceded (A).

2026-10-18.q: Why is maternity care "disproportionately affected" by the shortfall?
opts: Because insurers stopped covering pregnancy.
Because maternity consultants refused the new contract.
Because the Rotunda was closed.
Because women who want private maternity care have no private hospital to go to, so that income was earned in public hospitals.
2026-10-18.exp: "There are no private maternity hospitals in the State", so private maternity income came only from public hospitals — and that income is now lost.

2026-10-18.q: What is the function of the paragraph about the Rotunda Hospital?
opts: It gives an example of the non-compliance the review was checking and shows how it was resolved.
It argues that the Minister acted illegally.
It explains how the POCC began in 2023.
It proves that every hospital broke the rules.
2026-10-18.exp: It describes a case where consultants on public-only contracts still treated private patients and how pressure made the board concede — a concrete example of the issue.

2026-10-18-2.q: Which of the following best summarises the passage?
opts: Because a ministerial order was never approved by the Oireachtas, the old, lower merger threshold has returned, and recent deals may need to be reported.
The CCPC has fined companies for completing mergers without approval.
The Government has abolished the merger reporting rules.
The threshold for reporting mergers has permanently risen to €100 million.
2026-10-18-2.exp: The order lapsed on 30 September, so the €60 million threshold applies again. The CCPC promised not to take action (B), and the €100 million level lapsed (D).

2026-10-18-2.q: Why can the department not fix the problem immediately?
opts: Because the CCPC refuses to cooperate.
Because the minister has resigned.
Because companies have objected.
Because the law allows the thresholds to be changed only once a year.
2026-10-18-2.exp: New thresholds will come "as early as possible in 2027, given that the legislation permits only one adjustment annually".

2026-10-18-2.q: How would you describe the way the passage presents the Government's mistake?
opts: Angry and mocking.
Neutral and factual, explaining what went wrong and its consequences.
Full of praise for the department.
Humorous.
2026-10-18-2.exp: The passage reports the facts — the order, the missed approval, the review, the consequences — without emotional language.

2026-10-18-3.q: What is the main point of the passage?
opts: Kilmeaden residents voted to support the development.
The Government has approved a new technology campus near Waterford.
TikTok plans to build its own data centre in Kilmeaden.
After a large data-centre campus in Co Waterford was refused permission, politicians and campaigners called for limits on data centres not powered by renewable energy.
2026-10-18-3.exp: The refusal triggered calls for a moratorium and a national framework. Echelon, not TikTok, was the developer (C), and over 500 people objected (A).

2026-10-18-3.q: Why did the proposal include a café, shop, pharmacy, gym and childcare facility?
opts: Most likely to offer benefits to the local community and make the project more acceptable.
Because the planners required a pharmacy.
Because data centres need shops to operate.
Because TikTok asked for a gym.
2026-10-18-3.exp: A new village centre offers obvious community benefits; given the strong local opposition, it is reasonable to infer it was meant to make the plan more attractive. Nothing suggests the other reasons.

2026-10-18-3.q: How do Roderic O'Gorman's and David Cullinane's positions differ?
opts: Neither mentions energy.
Both want all data centres closed.
O'Gorman wants the moratorium brought back, while Cullinane calls for a broader national plan that balances different needs.
O'Gorman supports the Kilmeaden plan; Cullinane opposes it.
2026-10-18-3.exp: O'Gorman "advocated the reintroduction of the moratorium"; Cullinane stressed "a coherent national framework that balances electricity demand and climate commitments against the impact on local communities".

2026-10-18-4.q: Which statement best summarises the passage?
opts: Courts have banned objections to infrastructure projects.
Objectors must now pay the State to bring a case.
State bodies are paying large sums to settle legal challenges to infrastructure, which saves delays but may encourage more challenges.
The Dart+ West project has been cancelled.
2026-10-18-4.exp: The passage weighs both sides: settlements cost less than long delays (the official's view) but may "incentivise further litigation" (the critics' view).

2026-10-18-4.q: Why is the word "ransom" placed in quotation marks?
opts: Because a real kidnapping took place.
Because it is the official legal term for a settlement.
Because it is a critical description used by others, not a literal ransom.
Because Irish Rail used the word.
2026-10-18-4.exp: The quotation marks show it is a loaded, borrowed word from critics; settlements are legal agreements, not literal ransoms.

2026-10-18-4.q: Why does the writer mention the Greater Dublin Drainage scheme?
opts: To show that drainage projects are never delayed.
To give an example of a project bought by objectors.
To illustrate how long disputes can multiply a project's cost, supporting the official's argument for settling.
To argue that the State should never settle.
2026-10-18-4.exp: It is introduced as "illustrative": its cost rose from about €500 million to as much as €2.3 billion after extended disputes, backing the claim that delays are more expensive than settlements.
